html:
The Aryabhatiya is a Sanskrit treatise on mathematics and astronomy written around 499, in the late Gupta age, by Aryabhata, then 23 years old. It is the only work of his that survives and a landmark of Indian mathematics.

It is short: 121 verses in four parts.

  • A list of astronomical constants, written in a compact letter code for numbers.
  • Mathematics: place-value arithmetic, square and cube roots, geometry, series, a sine table and a method for solving equations in whole numbers.
  • Time reckoning and the motions of the planets.
  • The sphere: the shape of the Earth and sky, and eclipses.

It gives pi as 3.1416, says the Earth turns daily on its axis, and explains eclipses by shadows. Its verse form made it easy to memorise, so commentators such as Bhaskara I in the 7th century wrote long explanations.

The book shaped Indian astronomy for centuries. It was translated into Arabic, perhaps as the Zij al-Arjabhar, and Indian astronomy reached the astronomers of Baghdad under the Abbasids, alongside the flow of Greek learning into Baghdad.
